title.en: Impersonal sentences: мне хо́лодно, на́до, нельзя́

card: Many Russian sentences have no subject. The person who feels or needs something goes in the **dative**, and the predicate is a word in **-о** or a modal: **Мне хо́лодно.** **Тебе́ на́до отдохну́ть.** **Здесь нельзя́ кури́ть.** In the past and future add **бы́ло** / **бу́дет**: **Мне бы́ло хо́лодно.**

sections.body: English insists on a subject, even an empty one: *it is cold*, *it is necessary*. Russian is happy without one. It treats many states as things that *happen to* a person rather than things a person *is*, so that person appears in the dative, as an experiencer: **Мне ве́село** is closer to *for me it's fun* than to *I am cheerful*.

sections.title: Tense
sections.body:
The present has no verb. The past uses **бы́ло** and the future **бу́дет**, both neuter singular because there is no subject: **Мне бы́ло ску́чно.** **Тебе́ бу́дет интере́сно.** **Нам на́до бы́ло уйти́.** With a negation: **Мне не́ было ску́чно.**

Impersonal verbs use the neuter past: **Мне повезло́.** **Ему́ показа́лось.**

sections.title: на́до versus до́лжен
sections.body: **на́до / ну́жно** (impersonal + dative) express a general need: **Мне на́до рабо́тать.** **до́лжен / должна́ / должны́** (personal, agreeing with the subject) express obligation or duty: **Я до́лжен рабо́тать.** (*I must, it's my duty.*) **до́лжен** can also mean *supposed to*: **Он до́лжен прийти́ в пять.**

*I'm cold* is **мне хо́лодно**, not ~~я хо́лодный~~ (which would mean *I'm a cold person*, emotionally!). *I'm bored* is **мне ску́чно**; **я ску́чный** means *I'm boring*. These are some of the most noticeable English-speaker errors in Russian.

mistakes.why: The person experiencing a state is dative.
**на́до** is impersonal: dative of the person.

examples.en: We had a lot of fun.
